style="text;html=1;align=left;verticalAlign=top;resizable=0;points=[];autosize=1;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;" value="<font style="font-size:12px">1. Threads in same <b>warp</b> → execute in lockstep (same instruction, same cycle)<br>2. Threads in same <b>block</b> → CAN share data and synchronize<br>3. tr.td: Always exactly 32 threads. Fixed. Cannot change.
Hardware automatically. You NEVER create warps in code.
SIMT — all 32 execute SAME instruction at SAME clock cycle
If threads take different if/else paths → both paths serialize

Threads time-share cores (more threads than cores is GOOD)

div.span:
Hardware scheduler assigns blocks to SMs.
You have NO control over which SM gets which block.
More blocks than SMs = they queue and run as SMs free up.

path.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(22, 163, 74), rgb(39, 160, 83)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(22, 163, 74), rgb(39, 160, 83));

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(240, 253, 244), rgb(15, 26, 19)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(22, 163, 74), rgb(39, 160, 83));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 380px; height: 1px; padding-top: 425px; margin-left: 680px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.span:
Never split across multiple SMs.
Multiple blocks CAN share one SM (if resources fit).
This is why shared memory works — it's physically on the SM.
If block uses too many resources → fewer blocks per SM → worse perf.

path.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(22, 163, 74), rgb(39, 160, 83)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(22, 163, 74), rgb(39, 160, 83));

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(240, 253, 244), rgb(15, 26, 19)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(22, 163, 74), rgb(39, 160, 83));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 380px; height: 1px; padding-top: 672px; margin-left: 680px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.span:
SM has 4 warp schedulers. Each cycle, scheduler picks a ready warp
and issues ONE instruction to all 32 threads simultaneously.
This is how GPU hides memory latency: when one warp waits
for data, scheduler instantly switches to another ready warp.
This is why you want MORE threads than cores!

div.b: Thread → executes on a CUDA Core
div.span:
One thread uses one core for one clock cycle per instruction.
But threads TIME-SHARE cores (like OS threads share CPU cores).
128 cores per SM, but up to 1536 threads resident = 12× oversubscription.
This oversubscription is BY DESIGN (hides memory latency).

tr.td: Same warp → lockstep execution (same instruction, same cycle)
Same block → CAN share data (__shared__) and synchronize (__syncthreads)
Different blocks → CANNOT share data, CANNOT synchronize, execute in ANY order
One block lives on one SM — never split. This enables shared memory.
More threads than cores is GOOD — enables latency hiding via warp switching
Kernel launch is ASYNCHRONOUS — CPU continues immediately, use cudaDeviceSynchronize() to wait
CUDA errors are SILENT — always check with cudaGetLastError()
